title: Behavior trees: time limits and more
summary: Timeout, ReactiveSequence, ParallelDeadline, and tunable values.

steps.title: Timeout: don't hang forever
steps.say: A **Timeout** wraps one step and gives it a time limit in milliseconds. If the step is still RUNNING when time is up, the Timeout **halts** it (back to idle) and answers FAILURE. That turns "might never finish" into "fails after 3 seconds", which a Fallback can turn into plan B. It is the most useful pattern in an auto.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  fb["? Fallback"]:::idle
  to["Timeout 3 s"]:::idle
  aim["Aim"]:::idle
  backup["Backup path"]:::idle
  fb --> to
  to --> aim
  fb --> backup
  classDef idle fill:#6b7280,stroke:#9ca3af,color:#fff
  classDef running fill:#f59e0b,stroke:#b45309,color:#111
  classDef success fill:#16a34a,stroke:#166534,color:#fff
  classDef failure fill:#dc2626,stroke:#991b1b,color:#fff
diagram.caption: A Fallback: a Timeout around Aim, or the Backup path.

  classDef success fill:#16a34a,stroke:#166534,color:#fff

  linkStyle 0 stroke:#facc15,stroke-width:4px
  linkStyle 1 stroke:#facc15,stroke-width:4px
diagram.caption: Yellow lines are where this tick went; colours are each node's status.

steps.title: ReactiveSequence: keep checking
steps.say: A plain Sequence remembers where it was. A **ReactiveSequence** ticks **all** of its earlier children again on **every** tick. That is what you want for a condition that must stay true the whole time an action runs, like "drive only while we still hold a game piece".

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  rs["→ ReactiveSequence"]:::idle
  cond["Has game piece?"]:::idle
  drive["Drive path"]:::idle
  rs --> cond
  rs --> drive
  classDef idle fill:#6b7280,stroke:#9ca3af,color:#fff
  classDef running fill:#f59e0b,stroke:#b45309,color:#111
  classDef success fill:#16a34a,stroke:#166534,color:#fff
  classDef failure fill:#dc2626,stroke:#991b1b,color:#fff
diagram.caption: A condition followed by a long action.

steps.title: Tick 1
steps.say: A ReactiveSequence re-checks its earlier children on every tick. Tick 1: the condition passes and Drive path starts.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD

  cond["Has game piece? · SUCCESS"]:::success
  drive["Drive path · RUNNING"]:::running
  rs --> cond
  rs --> drive

  classDef failure fill:#dc2626,stroke:#991b1b,color:#fff
  linkStyle 0 stroke:#facc15,stroke-width:4px
  linkStyle 1 stroke:#facc15,stroke-width:4px
diagram.caption: Yellow lines are where this tick went; colours are each node's status.

steps.title: ParallelDeadline: at the same time
steps.say: A **ParallelDeadline** ticks all its children together. The **first** child is the deadline: when it finishes, all the others are halted and the node reports the deadline's result. "Drive this path, and drop the intake when the robot passes the marker" is exactly this: the path is the deadline.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  pd["⇉ ParallelDeadline"]:::idle
  path["Follow path"]:::idle
  intake["Intake on event"]:::idle
  pd --> path
  pd --> intake
  classDef idle fill:#6b7280,stroke:#9ca3af,color:#fff
  classDef running fill:#f59e0b,stroke:#b45309,color:#111
  classDef success fill:#16a34a,stroke:#166534,color:#fff
  classDef failure fill:#dc2626,stroke:#991b1b,color:#fff
diagram.caption: The path is the deadline.

steps.title: Tick 1
steps.say: A ParallelDeadline ticks all of its children together every tick. The first child, Follow path, is the deadline.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD

diagram.caption: Yellow lines are where this tick went; colours are each node's status.

steps.say: The deadline child finishes: SUCCESS. The others are halted, even though Intake on event never completed.

steps.title: Tunable values
steps.say: Any number can be **tunable**: changeable from the dashboard at the field, without editing the tree. Give the tree a setting of its own with a default, for example `wait_msec` = 500 (Arbor calls a tree's settings *ports*). Then, instead of typing 500 into a Sleep's `msec`, type the setting's name in braces: `{wait_msec}`. If you misspell the name, the auto refuses to load and tells you which box.

steps.title: Reading the colours in Arbor
steps.say: When Arbor is connected to a robot or the simulator, it draws exactly these colours: orange while a node is RUNNING, green for SUCCESS, red for FAILURE. If an auto stops somewhere unexpected, look for the node that is red, or the one that stayed orange. A Sequence that is red with its last children never lit up means an earlier child failed, and the rest were skipped on purpose.
